The filing identifies two operating businesses:

- **Clayton Homes:** Borrowings from Berkshire finance affiliates increased by **$6.6 billion** in 2024, reaching **$24.3 billion** at December 31, 2024. [Form 10-K, p. K-48]
- **Pilot Travel Centers:** Borrowed **$5.7 billion** from Berkshire insurance subsidiaries in March 2024 to repay third-party debt. Pilot subsequently repaid **$1.0 billion** of the affiliate borrowings during 2024. [Form 10-K, p. K-53]

- **Approximately $700 million**: Pfizer’s expected total cost of separating Upjohn, including legal-entity separation and transaction costs. **Approximately 75%** had been incurred from inception through December 31, 2021. (p. 26)
- **$434 million in 2020** and **$83 million in 2019**: separation-related costs incurred in those years and included in *Discontinued operations—net of tax*. They primarily covered professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities in finance, tax, legal and information systems, as well as investment-banking fees. (p. 65)

Source: Pfizer, *2021 Form 10-K*.

NVIDIA’s fiscal 2023 Form 10-K describes these effects:

- **Blocked products and support:** Sanctions and export controls imposed in response to the war blocked NVIDIA’s products, services and support from entering Russia, Belarus and certain regions of Ukraine. (p. 28)
- **Exit from Russia:** NVIDIA stopped direct sales to Russia during fiscal 2023 and closed its Russian business operations later that year. It noted that direct sales to Russia had been immaterial in fiscal 2022. (pp. 28, 37)
- **Sales and revenue:** The war had affected end-customer sales in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. NVIDIA also said revenue from partners selling into Russia **may have been negatively affected** by the war. (pp. 28, 37)

Source: *NVIDIA fiscal 2023 Form 10-K*, `NVDA_2023_10K.pdf`.

### Fiscal 2025 net sales

- **40%** came through direct distribution channels, such as Apple’s retail and online stores and direct sales force.
- **60%** came through indirect channels, such as third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers.  
  *(AAPL_2025_10K.pdf, PDF p. 5; printed p. 2)*

### Receivables as of September 27, 2025

- **12%** of total **trade receivables** was attributable to one customer.
- **34%** of total **trade receivables** was attributable to third-party cellular network carriers collectively.
- **46% and 23%** of total **vendor non-trade receivables** were attributable to two vendors, respectively. These receivables arose from Apple’s sales of components to manufacturing vendors.  
  *(AAPL_2025_10K.pdf, PDF p. 42; printed p. 39)*

As of December 31, 2023, Boeing reported these shares of its **total workforce**:

- **33%** — all union-represented employees, approximately 57,000 people.
- **21%** — represented by the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM).
- **10%** — represented by the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (SPEEA).
- **1%** — represented by the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW).

The three union-specific figures are shares of all employees, not shares of the union-represented group.

Source: Boeing 2023 Form 10-K, Human Capital and Risk Factors, pp. 2 and 9.

Apple identified the following results as having been adversely affected by weaker currencies against the U.S. dollar:

| Result | Fiscal 2024 | Fiscal 2023 | Currency effect |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Greater China net sales** | $66.952 billion | $72.559 billion | Weakness of the renminbi |
| **Japan net sales** | $25.052 billion | $24.257 billion | Weakness of the yen |
| **Rest of Asia Pacific net sales** | $30.658 billion | $29.615 billion | Net unfavorable effect of weaker foreign currencies |
| **Products gross margin and gross margin percentage** | $109.633 billion; 37.2% | $108.803 billion; 36.5% | Weaker foreign currencies, along with a different product mix, partially offset cost savings |

Some results increased despite the currency headwind. Apple did not separately quantify the currency effect on these results.

*Source: Apple fiscal 2024 Form 10-K, pp. 22 and 24 (PDF pp. 25 and 27).*

### Balances at January 25, 2026

- **$20.832 billion:** Total goodwill on NVIDIA’s consolidated balance sheet. Note 5 reports this as **$20.8 billion**, rounded. [FY2026 Form 10-K, pp. 53, 63]
- **$20.5 billion:** Goodwill allocated to the **Compute & Networking** reporting unit.
- **$370 million:** Goodwill allocated to the **Graphics** reporting unit. [p. 63]

### Added during fiscal 2026

- **$15.6 billion:** The total increase in goodwill during the year, all allocated to Compute & Networking. [p. 63]
- **$14.4 billion:** Goodwill recorded in connection with NVIDIA’s Groq technology license and hiring of certain Groq employees. It was primarily attributable to the workforce and future development of the licensed technology, allocated to Compute & Networking, and tax-deductible. [p. 61]

The Groq amount is part of the fiscal-year increase, not additional to it. The reported reporting-unit balances are rounded.

NVIDIA’s fiscal 2024 Form 10-K reports:

- **$2.2 billion** in total provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations. (p. 40)
- **$774 million** in inventory provisions charged to cost of revenue. NVIDIA’s inventory policy includes write-downs for excess or obsolete inventory. (pp. 58, 68)
- **Approximately $1.4 billion** in cost-of-revenue expense for inventory purchase obligations exceeding current demand projections, supplier charges, and cancellation and underutilization penalties. (p. 70)
- **$540 million** in provision releases resulting from sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations. (p. 40)

The $774 million and approximately $1.4 billion are components of the $2.2 billion total, not additional charges.

Apple’s filing dates the following developments to a day or month in **calendar 2025**:

- **April 23 — EU Digital Markets Act investigations:** The European Commission fined Apple **€500 million** and ordered it to remove restrictions preventing developers from steering users to alternatives outside the App Store. Separately, the Commission issued preliminary findings in its investigation of Apple’s contractual requirements for third-party developers and app marketplaces. Apple says it appealed the fine and order. *(Form 10-K, p. 18; PDF p. 21.)*

- **April 30 — Epic Games litigation:** A California federal court found Apple in violation of its 2021 injunction. It barred Apple from charging commissions or fees on purchases outside an app and from restricting developers’ guidance to users or interfering with users’ choices. The court also denied Apple’s motion to narrow or vacate the injunction and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for consideration of criminal contempt proceedings. *(p. 18; PDF p. 21.)*

- **September 2 — Google antitrust case:** Following its 2024 finding that Google violated U.S. antitrust law, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ordered remedies. Apple says the order remains subject to further proceedings and appeal; a reversal could lead to earlier DOJ-proposed restrictions on Google offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution. *(p. 14; PDF p. 17.)*

- **October — Epic Games appeal:** The Ninth Circuit heard oral arguments on Apple’s expedited appeal of the California court’s April decision. Apple’s request to stay that decision pending appeal had been denied. *(p. 18; PDF p. 21.)*

Berkshire said the COVID-19 pandemic severely disrupted air travel, commercial aerospace and supporting industries, prompting it to reassess the assets for impairment. Airlines delayed or cancelled aircraft orders, manufacturers reduced production rates, and PCC’s customers drew down inventories. Boeing 737 MAX production issues also contributed to declining aerospace sales in 2020. These factors sharply reduced demand for PCC’s products. (2021 Form 10-K, pp. K-49, K-89)

In its reassessment, Berkshire considered airlines’ announcements about future demand, employment and aircraft orders; manufacturers’ announced production cuts; and restructuring actions already taken or potentially needed. Reflecting the risks and uncertainties in aerospace, Berkshire **raised its discount rates and lowered its previous long-term cash-flow forecasts** in its discounted-cash-flow valuations. It noted that these estimates required significant judgment and that actual future results could differ materially from forecasts. (pp. K-63, K-89)

Apple identifies these causes of quarterly net-sales fluctuations:

- **Seasonal demand:** Holiday demand has historically helped make the first fiscal quarter stronger than other quarters.
- **Product and service introductions:** Their timing can significantly affect sales. After a launch, indirect distribution channels stock the new product; inventory of the older product often declines beforehand. Consumer and distributor anticipation of a launch can also affect sales.
- **Concentration in one product:** A decline in demand for the single product that accounts for a significant portion of net sales could substantially affect a quarter.
- **Unexpected developments:** These include lower-than-anticipated demand, problems with new product or service introductions, IT system failures or network disruptions, and failures by logistics, component-supply or manufacturing partners.

Source: *Apple 2023 Form 10-K*, pp. 4 and 15 (PDF pp. 7 and 18).

The securities are investments in private companies whose fair values are not readily determinable. They lack market prices and are inherently illiquid, so NVIDIA must use judgment to value them based on transactions in an inactive market.

Valuation can also require unobservable inputs, including volatility, expected time to liquidity, the risk-free rate, and rights and obligations specific to each security. Assessing impairment involves further judgment about factors such as the investee’s operating performance and market trends.

Source: NVIDIA FY2026 Form 10-K, pp. 38, 60, 66–67.

The increase reflected growth in balances in new and existing client accounts, supported by higher-yielding product offerings, and the full-year effect of First Republic deposits transferred to Asset & Wealth Management in the fourth quarter of 2023.

Source: JPMorgan Chase 2024 Form 10-K, PDF pp. 58 and 113.

Compared with fiscal 2025, Walmart attributed the fiscal 2026 gross profit rate increases to:

- **Company-wide, up 8 basis points:** disciplined inventory management in Walmart U.S. and growth in higher-margin businesses globally. (Form 10-K, p. 38)
- **Walmart U.S., up 22 basis points:** disciplined inventory management and growth in higher-margin businesses. (p. 39)
- **Sam’s Club U.S., up 4 basis points:** operational efficiencies and higher fuel margins. (p. 41)

Walmart International’s gross profit rate fell, so it is not included. (p. 40)

The increase was driven mainly by Pfizer’s acquisitions of **Arena, Global Blood Therapeutics (GBT), and Biohaven**. Pfizer provisionally recorded acquired IPR&D assets of $5.0 billion, $3.0 billion and $450 million, respectively. (2022 Form 10-K, Notes 2A and 10A, pp. 59–60 and 79.)

Partly offsetting the increase was a **$200 million impairment** of an IPR&D asset acquired with Array. The asset related to an unapproved indication for symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy caused by a mutation in the gene encoding lamin A/C. Pfizer said the impairment resulted from the Phase 3 trial reaching futility at a pre-planned interim analysis. (Note 4, p. 67.)

Compared with fiscal 2024, Walmart attributed the fiscal 2025 increases primarily to:

- **Company-wide:** Higher variable pay after exceeding planned performance, increased marketing, and higher depreciation. The ratio rose from 20.4% to 20.7%, or 36 basis points. (*Form 10-K, p. 39*)
- **Walmart U.S.:** Increased marketing, higher variable pay after exceeding planned performance, and higher depreciation. The ratio rose from 22.2% to 22.6%, or 44 basis points. (*p. 40*)
- **Sam’s Club U.S.:** Higher compensation-related expenses—including associate wage investments and higher variable pay after exceeding planned performance—and elevated technology spending. The ratio rose from 10.8% to 11.2%, or 44 basis points. (*p. 42*)

Walmart International’s ratio **decreased**, so it is not included among the increases. (*p. 41*) The percentages above are rounded; basis-point changes are those reported in the filing.

Pfizer attributed the **$1.052 billion favorable change** primarily to a swing in equity securities from $1.273 billion in net losses in 2022 to $1.590 billion in net gains in 2023, and to lower net interest expense. The 2023 gains included a $1.7 billion realized gain on its Telavant investment and $297 million in unrealized gains on Cerevel, partly offset by $292 million in unrealized losses on BioNTech.

Net interest expense fell from $987 million to $585 million. Interest expense increased, driven by the $31 billion of senior unsecured notes Pfizer issued in May 2023 to help finance the Seagen acquisition. That increase was more than offset by interest income earned from investing the net proceeds of the debt issuance.

These favorable factors were partly offset by higher intangible-asset impairment charges. Total asset-impairment charges rose from $421 million to $3.024 billion. The 2023 charges included $1.4 billion for etrasimod, reflecting changes in development plans and revenue expectations, and $964 million for Prevnar 13, reflecting updated forecasts and a transition to higher-serotype coverage.

*Source: Pfizer 2023 Form 10-K, p. 40 and Note 4, p. 73.*

The increase primarily reflected **$8.0 billion of IPR&D assets acquired with Metsera**. It was partly offset by $3.9 billion in IPR&D impairments and transfers from IPR&D to developed technology rights: $600 million for Padcev and $590 million for talazoparib (Talzenna). (2025 Form 10-K, Note 10A, p. 83.)

Pfizer attributed the impairment charges primarily to **changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts**. The $3.9 billion in IPR&D impairments included $1.6 billion for disitamab vedotin, $820 million for Tukysa (tucatinib) and $820 million for osivelotor. (Note 4, p. 70.)

- **Credit cards:** Loan growth from new accounts and higher revolving balances. (2025 Form 10-K, PDF pp. 68, 119)
- **Wholesale:** Higher commercial and industrial charge-offs, including in Technology, Media & Telecommunications and Healthcare, and estimated losses from borrower fraud in certain secured lending facilities. (PDF p. 126)
- **Asset & Wealth Management:** A third-quarter charge-off tied to a client-specific exposure. (PDF pp. 78–79)

ExxonMobil cited three main offsets to production growth:

- **Divestments** of producing assets.
- **Russia’s expropriation** of ExxonMobil’s interest in the Sakhalin-1 project.
- **Lower production entitlements** as prices rose; under some arrangements, fewer barrels were needed to recover costs.

Its separate upstream earnings analysis also cited **weather-related downtime** as a source of lost volume.

Source: *ExxonMobil 2022 Form 10-K*, PDF pp. 50, 52 and 54.

| Change | Approximate annual effect |
|---|---:|
| Brent crude price changes by **$1 per barrel** | **$700 million** change in earnings |
| Henry Hub gas price changes by **$0.10 per million British thermal units** | **$90 million** change in earnings |

| Worldwide assumed long-term return on pension assets falls by **0.5 percentage points** | **$150 million increase** in pension expense |

The three price sensitivities are for **2026**, measure after-tax Upstream consolidated and equity-company earnings, and exclude derivatives. The pension effect is **before tax**. The filing says benchmark price changes are only broad indicators of actual earnings effects. (*2025 Form 10-K*, pp. 62, 67; PDF pp. 64, 69.)

Separately, ExxonMobil attributes a **$6.1 billion** reduction in 2025 Upstream earnings versus 2024 to lower realizations, primarily crude prices. It attributes a **$1.3 billion** reduction in 2024 versus 2023 to price effects driven by lower gas realizations. (*Form 10-K*, pp. 45–46; PDF pp. 47–48.)

ExxonMobil acquired Pioneer on **May 3, 2024**. Its Form 10-K reports:

- **Size within ExxonMobil:** Pioneer represented **19% of consolidated total assets** at December 31, 2024, and **4% of consolidated total revenues** for 2024. These figures appear in the internal-control disclosure. (PDF p. 75)
- **Actual post-acquisition results:** From May 3 through December 31, Pioneer contributed **$17.008 billion in sales and other operating revenues** and **$1.710 billion in net income attributable to ExxonMobil**. (PDF p. 121)
- **Proved reserves:** The Pioneer acquisition was associated with an addition of **2.3 billion oil-equivalent barrels** to proved reserves in 2024. This is an addition during the year, not a separate year-end balance. (PDF p. 127)

The 4% revenue figure and the $17.008 billion amount come from separate disclosures; the filing does not reconcile them.

For broader operating context, ExxonMobil’s **total Permian** production averaged **1.185 million oil-equivalent barrels per day**, up approximately **570,000 per day** from 2023. It also reported a **$3.760 billion** upstream earnings increase from advantaged volume growth involving Pioneer, the heritage Permian and Guyana. Neither figure is Pioneer’s alone. (PDF pp. 49–50)

*Source: XOM_2024_10K.pdf; page references are PDF pages.*

Walmart identified the following **direct lapping effects** in its fiscal 2024 results. The prior-year items were among the factors in each change, not necessarily the sole cause.

| Fiscal 2024 result | Fiscal 2023 item lapped |
|---|---|
| **Consolidated gross profit rate:** up 27 basis points | Higher markdowns, primarily in Walmart U.S. (pp. 38, 41) |
| **Consolidated operating expenses as a percentage of net sales:** down 60 basis points | $3.3 billion of opioid-related legal settlement charges and $0.8 billion of Walmart International reorganization and restructuring charges. (pp. 38, 41) |
| **Return on investment:** up to 15.0% from 12.7% | The increase reflected higher operating income, primarily due to lapping the opioid-related settlement and reorganization and restructuring charges. (p. 38) |
| **Walmart U.S. gross profit rate:** up 20 basis points | Higher net markdowns. (p. 42) |
| **Walmart International operating expenses as a percentage of segment sales:** down 152 basis points | Business reorganization and restructuring charges related to Flipkart and Massmart. (p. 43) |
| **Sam’s Club gross profit rate:** up 55 basis points | Elevated markdowns. (p. 44) |

The filing also attributes the rise in consolidated operating margin and increases in segment operating income and consolidated net income to the preceding factors, which include these lapping effects. It does not separately quantify lapping’s contribution to those broader results. (pp. 38, 42–44)

*Source: Walmart fiscal 2024 Form 10-K.*

ExxonMobil attributed the rise to a **tight market for refined products**:

- **Demand recovered:** Gasoline and diesel demand returned to pre-pandemic levels, although jet-fuel demand remained below historical levels.
- **Refining capacity fell:** Refinery shutdowns and reduced investment during the pandemic constrained supply. Industry rationalization took more than 3 million barrels per day of refining capacity offline.
- **Other supply pressures:** Supply-chain constraints and low inventories added to the tightness.

The company said refining margins rose well above the top of their 2010–2019 historical range. *Source: ExxonMobil 2022 Form 10-K, PDF pp. 49, 55–56.*

Two filings report a cumulative excess at **December 31, 2021**:

| Company | Year-end excess | Source |
|---|---:|---|
| Berkshire Hathaway | Approximately **$1.9 billion** | 2021 Form 10-K, Note 1(k), PDF p. 79 |
| ExxonMobil | Estimated **$14.0 billion** | 2021 Form 10-K, Note 3, PDF p. 82 |

These are year-end balances, not changes during 2021 or effects on earnings. The Apple, JPMorgan Chase, Pfizer and Boeing filings do not state a corresponding year-end LIFO excess.

**Two filings report qualifying rating changes:**

| Filing | Rating agency | Reported change |
|---|---|---|
| **JPMorgan Chase** | **Standard & Poor’s (S&P)** | Upgraded ratings of the parent company and the listed subsidiaries on November 15, 2024. (2024 Form 10-K, p. 115; PDF p. 117) |
| **Boeing** | **Moody’s** | Downgraded Boeing’s long- and short-term ratings to Baa3 and P-3, respectively, in April 2024. (2024 Form 10-K, p. 44; PDF p. 46) |

I found no qualifying change reported in the other six filings. JPMorgan’s Moody’s affirmation and outlook changes, and S&P’s placement of Boeing under review, are not rating changes.

**Three filings** identify a collective chief operating decision maker:

- **JPMorgan Chase:** The **Operating Committee**, whose members act collectively as the CODM. (*JPM_2024_10K.pdf*, Note 32, PDF p. 315)
- **Berkshire Hathaway:** An **unnamed group** comprising the chairman and CEO, the vice chairman of insurance operations, and the vice chairman of non-insurance operations. (*BRK_2024_10K.pdf*, Note 26, PDF p. 110)
- **ExxonMobil:** The **Management Committee**, comprising the CEO, CFO and two senior vice presidents serving as contact executives for the Upstream and Product Solutions businesses. (*XOM_2024_10K.pdf*, Note 18, PDF p. 110)

NVIDIA, Pfizer and Boeing each identify an individual executive as CODM. Apple and Walmart refer to a CODM but do not identify who fills the role in their fiscal 2024 segment notes. (*NVDA_2024_10K.pdf*, p. 78; *PFE_2024_10K.pdf*, p. 111; *BA_2024_10K.pdf*, p. 118; *AAPL_2024_10K.pdf*, p. 49; *WMT_2024_10K.pdf*, p. 78; all PDF pages)

Apple’s fiscal 2021 Form 10-K reports these interest amounts:

| Amount | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **$2.645 billion** | Total fiscal 2021 interest expense reported in other income/(expense), net. (p. 41) |
| **$2.6 billion** | Fiscal 2021 interest expense specifically recognized on term debt, reported on a rounded basis. This overlaps with the total above. (p. 45) |
| **$2.687 billion** | Cash paid for interest during fiscal 2021, as reported in the cash-flow statement. The filing does not break this amount out by instrument. (p. 33) |
| **$39.5 billion** | Total future interest payments associated with the outstanding notes as of September 25, 2021. (p. 24) |
| **$2.9 billion** | The portion of those future notes interest payments payable within 12 months. It is included in the $39.5 billion total. (p. 24) |
| **$186 million** | The *annualized increase* in interest expense that a hypothetical 100-basis-point rise in market rates would cause on debt outstanding as of September 25, 2021. It is not an actual expense or a total payment. (p. 26) |

The filing does not separately quantify commercial-paper interest expense or future interest payments. In particular, the difference between the first two figures cannot be treated as a precise commercial-paper charge, because the term-debt figure is rounded. (pp. 44–45)

*Page references are to the printed page numbers in Apple’s 2021 Form 10-K.*

For fiscal 2023, which ended September 30, Apple’s Form 10-K reports:

- **$14.996 billion declared:** Dividends and dividend equivalents recorded as a reduction to retained earnings. The amount declared was **$0.94 per share or restricted stock unit (RSU)** for the year. (p. 31)
- **$15.025 billion paid:** Cash payments for dividends and dividend equivalents, reported in the cash-flow statement. Management also describes this as **$15.0 billion**, rounded. (pp. 20, 32)
- **$0.23 and $0.24 per share:** The quarterly cash dividend rate was $0.23 before Apple raised it to $0.24 beginning in May 2023. The $0.24 rate remained in effect at fiscal year-end. (pp. 20, 25)

The declared and paid totals are different measures and should not be added together.

For the fiscal year ended September 24, 2022, Apple’s Form 10-K reports:

- **Approximately 41 million shares withheld** from vested RSUs to cover employees’ income and other employment taxes. Apple valued the shares using its closing stock price on the respective vesting dates. (p. 47)
- **$6.4 billion** in total payments to taxing authorities for employees’ tax obligations, as reported in the RSU note. (p. 47)
- **$6.223 billion** in financing cash outflows for “payments for taxes related to net share settlement of equity awards.” (p. 33)
- **$2.971 billion** charged against common stock and additional paid-in capital, and **$3.454 billion** against retained earnings, for stock withheld in net settlement of equity awards. Together, these are a **$6.425 billion equity reduction**, not additional tax payments. (p. 32)
- **85.228 million shares issued, net of shares withheld for employee taxes**. This is net issuance, not the number of shares withheld. (p. 46)

The cited disclosures do not reconcile the $6.4 billion and $6.223 billion payment figures. They describe related activity and should not be added together.

**Three filings qualify:** NVIDIA, Apple and Walmart. The amounts below are authorization ceilings, not the amounts actually repurchased.

| Company | Authorization during fiscal 2023 | Amount, $ billions |
|---|---|---:|
| **NVIDIA** | On May 23, 2022, the board increased and extended its existing program to permit repurchases up to $15 billion through December 2023. | **15** |
| **Apple** | A new program for up to $90 billion was announced May 4, 2023. | **90** |
| **Walmart** | A new $20 billion program was approved in November 2022, replacing the previous program beginning November 21. | **20** |

Sources: `NVDA_2023_10K.pdf`, p. 34; `AAPL_2023_10K.pdf`, p. 21; `WMT_2023_10K.pdf`, p. 45. Page numbers are PDF pages.

**The other five do not qualify based on their filings:**

- **JPMorgan Chase:** Its $30 billion program was announced in 2022; purchases resumed under it in 2023. (`JPM_2023_10K.pdf`, p. 101)
- **Berkshire Hathaway:** Its existing program did not specify a fixed dollar authorization. The $9.2 billion reported for 2023 was the amount actually spent. (`BRK_2023_10K.pdf`, pp. 35, 60)
- **Pfizer:** Its $10 billion program was authorized in 2018; approximately $3.3 billion remained at the end of 2023. (`PFE_2023_10K.pdf`, p. 100)
- **ExxonMobil:** Its program was expanded to $50 billion in 2022. The 2023 filing described a *future expected* pace increase after the Pioneer transaction closed, not a 2023 authorization. (`XOM_2023_10K.pdf`, p. 32)
- **Boeing:** The filing reports no qualifying new authorization; its fourth-quarter share acquisitions were employee tax-withholding transfers, not open-market program purchases. (`BA_2023_10K.pdf`, p. 24)

For fiscal 2024, ended September 28, Apple’s Form 10-K reports:

- **499 million shares for $95.0 billion:** the narrative description of common stock repurchased during the year. (p. 44)
- **499,372,000 shares:** the more precise repurchase count in the shares-outstanding reconciliation, reported there as 499,372 thousand shares. (p. 44)
- **$95.846 billion:** the deduction for common stock repurchased in the statement of shareholders’ equity, under retained earnings/accumulated deficit. (p. 32)
- **$94.949 billion:** the cash outflow for repurchases of common stock in the statement of cash flows. (p. 33)

These are overlapping presentations, not amounts to add together. The cited passages do not reconcile the different dollar figures.

Berkshire’s 2022 Form 10-K identifies four relevant effects:

- **Insurance investment income:** Rising rates increased interest income. Interest and other investment income rose by $1.1 billion, also reflecting income from the acquired Alleghany insurance subsidiaries. After-tax insurance investment earnings rose by $1.7 billion, reflecting higher rates and increased dividend income. (pp. K-33, K-40)
- **Variable-annuity guarantee reinsurance:** The contracts produced a $117 million pre-tax underwriting gain. Berkshire attributed the earnings primarily to the combined effects of interest-rate increases and changes in securities markets; it did not isolate the rate effect. (p. K-40)
- **Real estate brokerage and mortgage services:** Rising rates reduced homeowner refinancing activity. Mortgage-services closed transaction volume fell 40%, reducing revenues and margins. This contributed to a $287 million decline in the real estate brokerage business’s after-tax earnings; lower brokerage transaction volume was another factor. (p. K-45)
- **Building products and homebuilding, including Clayton Homes:** Higher rates contributed to slowing demand for new-home construction in the fourth quarter of 2022. (pp. K-16, K-50)

As of **December 31, 2021**, JPMorgan Chase reported these loans under COVID-19 payment deferral programs:

**Retained loan portfolios**
- **Consumer:** approximately **$1.3 billion**, predominantly residential real estate.
- **Wholesale:** approximately **$107 million**.

**Principal balances by business**
- **Home Lending:** **$1.1 billion**
- **Card:** **$46 million**
- **Auto:** **$115 million**

The business-level figures overlap with the broader consumer-portfolio disclosure and should not be added to it.

*Source: JPMorgan Chase 2021 Form 10-K, PDF pp. 67–68, 114 and 120.*

- **U.S. comparable sales — meaningful.** The measure indicates sales performance at existing stores and clubs, including e-commerce. - **Return on investment (ROI) — meaningful.** ROI helps investors assess how effectively Walmart deploys its assets. Walmart says its adjustments to operating income and total assets make ROI a more accurate measure of key-asset deployment, and more meaningful to investors, than return on assets. (pp. 38–39)
- **Free cash flow — important.** It measures Walmart’s ability to generate additional cash from business operations and helps evaluate financial performance. It also provides supplemental information to the consolidated statements of cash flows. (p. 40)
- **Sam’s Club results excluding fuel — useful.** The filing presents net sales, sales growth, operating income and operating income as a percentage of net sales excluding fuel. This helps investors understand the effect of fuel sales, whose results are affected by volatile fuel prices; management also uses it to better measure underlying segment results. (p. 43)

The filing distinguishes the initial exchange gain from the broader net Visa-related gain; **they are not additive**.

### Financial results

- **Exchange gain:** JPMorgan recorded an initial **$7.990 billion gain**—rounded to $8.0 billion—based on the fair value of the Class C shares received. After other second-quarter Visa activity, including changes in the fair values of the Class C shares and derivatives and dividends, the **net Visa-related gain was $7.9 billion**. It increased Corporate other income and noninterest revenue. (Form 10-K, pp. 60, 200, 228)
- **Foundation contribution:** The Firm contributed **$1.0 billion** of Class C shares to the JPMorgan Chase Foundation in the second quarter, recording the contribution as noninterest expense. It sold the remaining Class C shares in the second and third quarters. (pp. 200, 228)
- **Cash-flow reconciliation:** The statement of cash flows deducted the **$7.990 billion initial gain** from net income when reconciling it to operating cash flow. This was an adjustment for the exchange gain, not itself a cash outflow. (p. 176)
- **Taxes:** The Visa gain and contribution were among the factors affecting the income-and-expense mix that increased the Firm’s effective tax rate to **22.1% in 2024 from 19.6% in 2023**. The filing does not separately quantify their tax effect. (p. 62)

### Market risk

The Class C exposure elevated **average and maximum Corporate, Other and Total risk-management value-at-risk (VaR)**. The reported figures below are for the full portfolios, not amounts attributable solely to Visa:

| One-day VaR, approximately 95% confidence | 2024 average / maximum | 2023 average / maximum |
|---|---:|---:|
| Corporate | $23m / $102m | $12m / $17m |
| Other | $25m / $101m | $14m / $22m |
| Total | $47m / $91m | $43m / $57m |

The Firm said the second-quarter rise and subsequent fall in daily VaR were primarily driven by changes in its Class C exposure. The **$4 million increase in average Total VaR** also reflected other factors, including increased credit protection; it was not attributed entirely to Visa. (pp. 143–144)

The Firm retained **18.6 million Class B-2 shares** at year-end at a nominal carryover basis. Their transfer restrictions and ultimate conversion rate remained subject to Visa litigation; the rate at December 31 was **1.5430 Class A shares per B-2 share**. (p. 200)

- **Other purchase obligations: $14.8 billion**, including **$7.0 billion payable within 12 months**. These primarily comprise noncancelable commitments for capital assets, including manufacturing assets, and for supplier arrangements, licensed intellectual property and content, and distribution rights. *(p. 25; PDF p. 28.)*

These are off-balance-sheet commitments to buy goods or services, primarily under supplier arrangements and for licensed intellectual property, content and distribution rights. This total includes all future payments under those commitments, not just payments due after one year. The note does not separately label a 12-month amount. *(Note 12, p. 46; PDF p. 49.)*

Boeing reported 348 commercial-airplane deliveries in 2024, down from 528 in 2023, including intercompany deliveries. It linked the lower deliveries to:

- **Safety and quality improvement actions** following the January 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident, including slowing production.
- **Supply-chain constraints.**
- **The IAM 751 work stoppage**, which paused production of several models and significantly reduced deliveries in the second half of 2024.
- **Delays associated with business-class seats**, which adversely affected 787 deliveries in 2024.

The year-over-year comparison also includes one 747 delivery in 2023 and none in 2024; Boeing delivered the final 747 in February 2023.

*Source: Boeing 2024 Form 10-K, PDF pp. 26, 35, 37, 39 and 44.*

Walmart attributed the fiscal 2023 gross profit rate declines primarily to the following, compared with fiscal 2022:

- **Company-wide — down 98 basis points:** U.S. markdowns and merchandise mix, higher supply-chain costs, and inflation-related last-in, first-out (LIFO) charges at Sam’s Club. *(p. 40)*
- **Walmart U.S. — down 85 basis points:** Net markdowns, a shift toward lower-margin product categories, and increased supply-chain costs. *(p. 41)*
- **Walmart International — down 50 basis points:** Continued growth in lower-margin formats and channels in China, and shifts toward lower-margin merchandise categories. *(p. 42)*
- **Sam’s Club — down 155 basis points:** Inventory write-downs, elevated supply-chain and e-commerce fulfillment costs, and inflation-related LIFO charges. *(p. 43)*

As background, Walmart also said supply-chain disruptions contributed to higher-than-normal inventories and high inflation affected merchandise costs. *(Walmart fiscal 2023 Form 10-K, p. 36)*

ExxonMobil said energy markets normalized from their 2022 highs:

- **Crude oil:** Growing liquids supply helped meet record demand, while higher inventories weighed on prices in the first half of 2023.
- **Natural gas:** Higher supply and lower demand pushed storage levels in the United States and Europe above historical averages. Gas prices fell significantly during the first nine months.

Lower realizations reduced 2023 Upstream earnings by **$14.29 billion** compared with 2022. ExxonMobil also reported a separate $2.38 billion unfavorable mark-to-market impact.

*Source: ExxonMobil 2023 Form 10-K, pp. 49 and 51 (PDF pp. 51 and 53).*

Two filings state a qualifying amount:

Subsequent 2022 earnings would supplement that capacity. (*2021 Form 10-K*, Note 26, PDF p. 282.)
- **Berkshire Hathaway: up to approximately $30 billion.** Its principal insurance subsidiaries could declare that amount in ordinary dividends during 2022 without prior regulatory approval. (*2021 Form 10-K*, Note 15, PDF p. 92.)

I did not find a corresponding year-end program balance in the 2025 filings of NVIDIA, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, Berkshire Hathaway or ExxonMobil. That does not establish that they had no such programs.

**Two filings state qualifying amounts:**

| Company | Fiscal 2022 year-end | Indefinitely reinvested earnings |
|---|---|---|
| **NVIDIA** | January 30, 2022 | Approximately **$1.05 billion** in Israel and **$232 million** in the United Kingdom. [NVIDIA 2022 Form 10-K, p. 75] |
| **Pfizer** | December 31, 2022 | **$60.0 billion** of unremitted earnings of international subsidiaries. [Pfizer 2022 Form 10-K, PDF p. 77] |

The other six filings do not give a qualifying earnings amount. Berkshire Hathaway, ExxonMobil and Boeing discuss indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings without quantifying them. Walmart’s approximately **$3 billion** is an unrecorded deferred tax liability, not the earnings themselves. [BRK, PDF p. 104; XOM, PDF p. 118; BA, PDF p. 79; WMT, PDF p. 73]

**Two filings** report qualifying issuances:

| Filing | Issuance date | Preferred stock issued |
|---|---|---|
| **JPMorgan Chase** | **March 12, 2024** | $2.5 billion of Series NN fixed-rate reset, non-cumulative preferred stock, represented by depositary shares. *JPM_2024_10K.pdf*, PDF pp. 293–294. |
| **Boeing** | **October 31, 2024** | 115 million depositary shares representing 5.75 million shares of 6.00% Series A mandatory convertible preferred stock. *BA_2024_10K.pdf*, PDF p. 110. |

JPMorgan’s Series OO issuance occurred in **2025**, after its fiscal year-end. Boeing’s **October 30, 2024** issuance was common stock, not the preferred stock.

The other six filings do not report a qualifying issuance of their own preferred stock in fiscal 2024.

Five filings state amounts for leases that had not yet commenced at fiscal year-end:

| Company | Future payments or commitments ($ millions) | 2023 Form 10-K source |
|---|---:|---|
| NVIDIA | **463** — operating leases | Note 3, PDF p. 67 |
| Apple | **544** | Note 8, PDF p. 46 |
| JPMorgan Chase | **420** — operating leases | Note 18, PDF p. 277 |
| ExxonMobil | **4,063** — operating; **2,256** — finance | Note 11, PDF p. 100 |
| Boeing | **430** | Note 12, PDF p. 84 |

ExxonMobil describes its two amounts as **undiscounted commitments**.

I did not find a separately stated amount for not-yet-commenced leases in the Berkshire Hathaway, Pfizer or Walmart filings. That does not establish that those companies had no such leases.

**Two filings disclose a qualifying year-end balance**, both as of December 31, 2022:

| Company | Recorded remediation liability ($ millions) | Source |
|---|---:|---|
| ExxonMobil | **$730** | 2022 Form 10-K, environmental liabilities, PDF p. 70 |
| Boeing | **$752** | 2022 Form 10-K, Note 13, PDF p. 87 |

I found no separately stated qualifying balance in the other six filings: NVIDIA, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, Berkshire Hathaway, Pfizer or Walmart. That is not a finding that their liabilities were zero.

Pfizer says it accrued for remediation at the former Wyeth facility in Bound Brook, but does not state the amount in that disclosure (PDF p. 102). Berkshire’s stated asbestos and environmental claim liabilities concern insurance or reinsurance claims, rather than cleanup of its own sites (PDF pp. 63–64).

**Two filings qualify:**

| Company | FY2023 advertising expense or costs | Source |
|---|---:|---|
| Pfizer | Approximately **$3.7 billion** | 2023 Form 10-K, Note 1.J, PDF p. 70 |
| Walmart | **$4.1 billion** | 2023 Form 10-K, Note 1, PDF p. 64 |

I found no qualifying company-wide amount in the other six filings. JPMorgan Chase reports **marketing** expense, not advertising expense; Berkshire Hathaway discusses reduced GEICO advertising but does not give a company-wide advertising total. (JPMorgan 10-K, PDF p. 59; Berkshire 10-K, PDF pp. 39–40.)

Three filings state a qualifying Moody’s long-term rating:

| Filing | Rating | Scope and reported date |
|---|---:|---|
| JPMorgan Chase | **A1** | Parent company’s long-term issuer rating as of December 31, 2022. Moody’s upgraded it from A2 on September 29, 2022. [JPM_2022_10K.pdf, PDF p. 106] |
| Pfizer | **A1** | Senior unsecured long-term debt rating, described as current in the filing. Moody’s upgraded it from A2 in November 2022. [PFE_2022_10K.pdf, PDF p. 50] |
| Walmart | **Aa2** | Rating on its rated series of outstanding long-term debt as of January 31, 2022. [WMT_2022_10K.pdf, PDF pp. 44–45] |

I did not find a qualifying Moody’s long-term rating in the NVIDIA, Apple, Berkshire Hathaway, ExxonMobil or Boeing filings. For example, Berkshire reports other agencies’ ratings for its insurance subsidiaries, while Boeing discusses its ratings without giving a Moody’s long-term grade. [BRK_2022_10K.pdf, PDF p. 4; BA_2022_10K.pdf, PDF p. 45]

**Four filings identify a qualifying acquisition:**

| Filing | Company acquired | Completion date | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Walmart | VIZIO Holding Corp. | December 2024 | WMT 2025 10-K, PDF p. 34 |
| Berkshire Hathaway | Bell Laboratories, LLC | July 31, 2025 | BRK 2025 10-K, PDF p. 17 |
| Pfizer | Metsera | November 13, 2025 | PFE 2025 10-K, PDF p. 73 |
| Boeing | Spirit AeroSystems Holdings, Inc. | December 8, 2025 | BA 2025 10-K, PDF p. 27 |

Boeing acquired **all of Spirit’s outstanding shares**, although Spirit sold certain assets to Airbus concurrently. (BA 2025 10-K, PDF pp. 27, 75.)

**Why the others do not qualify:** NVIDIA reports acquisitions but does not name the acquired companies; Apple’s filing does not identify a qualifying named acquisition. JPMorgan Chase’s 2025 settlement concerned certain First Republic assets acquired in **2023**. ExxonMobil acquired technology and assets from Superior Graphite in 2025, while its acquisition of Pioneer closed in **2024**. (NVDA, PDF pp. 34, 65; JPM, p. 314; XOM, pp. 56, 114.)

Berkshire’s OxyChem acquisition is also excluded: it closed on **January 2, 2026**, after its fiscal year ended. (BRK, PDF p. 17.)
